title: Skardu in Autumn and Kashmir's Green Hills: When to Go and What You'll See
summary: Golden poplars around Shangrila in autumn and misty pine hills in summer. When Skardu's colours peak, how to get there, and where to find Kashmir-style scenery near Islamabad.
image_alt: Autumn trees in red and gold below snow peaks near Skardu, beside green pine-covered hills in Kashmir
body:
Northern Pakistan looks completely different depending on when you go. In autumn, the valleys around Skardu turn gold and red under snow-capped Karakoram peaks. In summer, the hills of Kashmir are deep green, with pine forest and clouds drifting through the valleys. These two short videos from our [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/pastenlighten/) show both, and this guide explains when to go and how to plan each trip.

## Skardu in autumn

Skardu sits in a wide valley of the Indus River in Gilgit-Baltistan, surrounded by bare mountains and sand dunes. For most of the year the scenery is shades of brown, grey and blue. Then, for a few weeks in autumn, the lines of poplar trees along the fields and lakes turn bright yellow, and apricot and willow trees add orange and red.

### When the colours are at their best

The colours usually peak from **mid-October to early November**. The exact timing moves by a week or two each year depending on the weather, and higher villages change first. By mid-November most trees have lost their leaves, and winter cold sets in.

### Where to see them

- **Shangrila and Lower Kachura Lake:** the red-roofed resort and its still lake are the classic autumn view, about 30 to 45 minutes from Skardu town
- **Upper Kachura Lake:** a quieter, deep-blue lake with orchards and walking paths around the shore
- **Shigar Valley:** villages, fields and the restored Shigar Fort, with poplar-lined roads all the way
- **The Indus valley road and Sarfaranga cold desert:** golden trees against sand dunes and river channels
- **Satpara Lake:** just south of Skardu, on the road towards Deosai

### Getting there in autumn

We recommend **flying from Islamabad to Skardu**. The flight is short and scenic, but it depends on the weather, so keep a spare day before any onward connection. In autumn the road options are limited: the Babusar Pass usually closes for winter, and the UK currently advises against all travel on the section of the Karakoram Highway between Mansehra and the N15 junction, the main alternative route. Foreign visitors must register with the local authorities in Gilgit-Baltistan, which we arrange for our guests.

### Good to know

- Days are often clear and sunny, but mornings and nights can be close to freezing by November, so bring warm layers, a hat and gloves
- Deosai National Park is usually only open in summer, so it is not part of an autumn trip. See our [Deosai guide](blog/deosai-national-park-travel-guide.html)
- Many hotels and cafés are much quieter after the summer season, which makes autumn a calm time to visit
- Early morning and the hour before sunset give the best light for photographs of the lakes and trees

## Kashmir's green hills

Kashmir is a completely different landscape from Skardu: lower, greener and softer. Pine and deodar forest covers the ridges, and after rain the clouds settle in the valleys below the hilltops. The hills are greenest in summer, from about June to September. July and August bring the monsoon, which is when the clouds are most dramatic but also when landslides can close roads, so leave time in your plan.

### Before you go: check the travel advice

If you are visiting from abroad, check your government's travel advice before planning a trip to Azad Jammu and Kashmir. At the time of writing, the UK advises against all but essential travel to Azad Jammu and Kashmir and against all travel within 10 miles of the Line of Control. Canada advises avoiding all travel there. Much of the upper Neelum Valley lies close to the Line of Control. Travel insurance may not cover you if you travel against this advice.

Pakistani travellers visit Azad Kashmir in large numbers, especially in summer. Read our [Neelum Valley and Sharda guide](blog/neelum-valley-sharda-travel-guide.html), and ask us about current road conditions before you go.

### Kashmir-style scenery near Islamabad

If Azad Kashmir is not an option for you, the **Murree Hills and the Galiyat** (Ayubia, Nathia Gali and Dunga Gali) have the same pine-covered ridges, cool air and clouds in the valleys. They are about one to three hours' drive from Islamabad and make an easy one- or two-day trip from the capital. Nathia Gali and Ayubia are in Abbottabad District, so check the current advice for that area too.

## Which trip is right for you?

- **Best time:** Skardu in autumn: Mid-October to early November. Kashmir's green hills: June to September.
- **Scenery:** Skardu in autumn: Golden trees, lakes, snow peaks and desert. Kashmir's green hills: Pine forest, green ridges, clouds and rivers.
- **Getting there:** Skardu in autumn: Fly Islamabad to Skardu (weather permitting). Kashmir's green hills: By road from Islamabad.
- **Ideal length:** Skardu in autumn: 4 to 6 days. Kashmir's green hills: 2 to 5 days.
- **Good to know:** Skardu in autumn: Cold mornings; Deosai closed. Kashmir's green hills: Monsoon rain and landslides in July–August; check travel advice.

## Frequently asked questions

### When is the best time to see autumn colours in Skardu?

Usually from mid-October to early November, when poplar, apricot and willow trees turn gold, orange and red. The exact peak moves by a week or two each year with the weather, and by mid-November most leaves have fallen.

### Can you visit Skardu in November?

Yes. Early November often still has colour, clear skies and very few crowds, but mornings and nights are close to freezing. Deosai is closed by then, and flights can be cancelled in bad weather, so keep a spare day in your plan.

### How do you get to Skardu in autumn?

We recommend flying from Islamabad to Skardu. The Babusar Pass road usually closes for winter, and the UK currently advises against all travel on the Karakoram Highway between Mansehra and the N15 junction, which is the other road route.

### Can foreign tourists visit Azad Kashmir?

Check your government's advice first. The UK advises against all but essential travel to Azad Jammu and Kashmir and against all travel within 10 miles of the Line of Control, and Canada advises avoiding all travel there. If that applies to you, the Murree Hills and the Galiyat near Islamabad have similar pine ridges and clouds in the valleys.

We plan northern trips privately around your dates, so tell us when you would like to travel on [WhatsApp](https://wa.me/923344770455) and we will suggest the best route for the season. For more planning help, see our [month-by-month guide to northern Pakistan](blog/best-time-visit-northern-pakistan-month-by-month.html) and [Skardu travel guide](blog/skardu-travel-guide.html).

title: Lahore Fort at Night: A Sufi Evening in Old Lahore
summary: Lahore Fort lit up after dark, a costumed Mughal-court performance, and the city's Sufi music and dhamal. What our Sufi Night tour is like, and how to plan your own evening.
image_alt: Lahore Fort courtyard lit up at night, with performers in Mughal costume in front of five red-curtained arches
body:
Lahore changes after dark. The traffic thins, the old monuments are lit in warm gold, and the city's Sufi traditions come alive with drums, music and devotion. This short video was filmed by our team on a recent Sufi Night tour, at Lahore Fort, and it is one of our favourite moments to share on [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/pastenlighten/).

## Lahore Fort after dark

By day, Lahore Fort (the Shahi Qila) is busy with school groups and visitors, and the sun on the red sandstone and marble can be fierce. At night it feels completely different. Lights pick out the carved arches and domed pavilions, the air is cooler, and the courtyards become a stage.

In the video you can see performers in Mughal costume in front of five red-curtained arches, re-creating a scene from the royal court while the audience watches from the courtyard. It is a lovely way to understand how these buildings were used, not just how they look.

The Walled City of Lahore Authority runs evening visits and night tours at the fort, with lighting, storytelling and live performances. The schedule, days and ticket prices change from season to season, so we check them for each group and plan the evening around them.

## Lahore's Sufi nights

Sufism has shaped Lahore for nearly a thousand years. The city grew up around the shrine of Data Ganj Bakhsh (Data Darbar), and its saints are still honoured every week with music and devotion. A Sufi night is not a show put on for tourists: it is a living tradition that you are welcome to watch with respect.

- **Data Darbar:** the shrine of the 11th-century saint Ali Hujwiri, one of the most visited Sufi shrines in South Asia, busy and atmospheric in the evening
- **Shah Jamal:** a small shrine famous for its night of dhol drumming and dhamal, the spinning devotional dance, in the tradition of the legendary drummer Pappu Sain
- **Qawwali:** devotional songs with harmonium, tabla and clapping, performed at shrines on many evenings

## What our Sufi Night tour includes

- An evening visit to Data Darbar
- Dhol and dhamal at the Shah Jamal shrine
- Qawwali music where it is being performed that night
- A local expert guide who explains the history, the rituals and what is happening around you
- All entry tickets, a shoe basket and a bottle of water

The tour usually starts at about 9:50 pm. We can add time at Lahore Fort in the evening when its night programme fits your dates, just as we did on the tour in the video. Prices start from US$40 per person for a solo traveller and drop for groups; see the [Night Sufi Shrine Tour](tours/sufi-night.html) for details.

## Tips for a Sufi evening in Lahore

- Dress modestly, with shoulders and knees covered. Women may want a light scarf
- Wear shoes that are easy to slip off, because shoes come off inside shrines
- Carry a little cash in small notes, and keep your phone and wallet in a front pocket in the crowds
- Ask before photographing people, and put the camera away during prayers
- October to March is the most comfortable season for evenings out in Lahore
- For the rest of your stay, see our [one-day Lahore itinerary](blog/one-day-in-lahore-itinerary.html) and [what to wear in Lahore](blog/what-to-wear-in-lahore.html)

## Frequently asked questions

### Can you visit Lahore Fort at night?

Yes. The Walled City of Lahore Authority runs evening visits and night tours at Lahore Fort, usually with lighting, storytelling and live performances. Days, times and ticket prices change by season, so check the current schedule before you go, or ask us and we will check for you.

### What happens on a Sufi night in Lahore?

Our Sufi Night tour visits Data Darbar in the evening, then the Shah Jamal shrine for dhol drumming and dhamal, the spinning devotional dance, with qawwali music where it is being performed that night.

### What should I wear?

Dress modestly, with shoulders and knees covered. Women may want a light scarf for the shrines. Shoes come off inside shrines, so wear shoes that are easy to take off and put on.

### Is the Sufi Night tour private?

Yes, it is private for you and your group by default, with an English- or Urdu-speaking guide. You can also join a shared small group.

Tell us your dates on [WhatsApp](https://wa.me/923344770455) and we will check what is happening at the shrines and at Lahore Fort that week, and plan the evening around it. You can pair it with our [Lahore Fort and Walled City heritage walk](tours/lahore-heritage-walk.html) during the day.

title: Badshahi Mosque, Lahore: Its Story, Visiting Tips and What Our Guests Say
summary: Built by Aurangzeb in just two years and the world's largest mosque for over 300 years. The short history of Lahore's Badshahi Masjid, practical tips for your visit, and what our guests say about seeing it with a local guide.
image_alt: Three of our guests standing in the courtyard of Badshahi Mosque in Lahore, with its red sandstone gate and white marble domes behind them
body:
Of all the places we show our guests in Lahore, Badshahi Mosque is the one they talk about most. You climb the steps, walk through the great gate, and the courtyard suddenly opens out in front of you: red sandstone, three white marble domes and a minaret at each corner. This short reel is made from real photos of our guests and real lines from their Google reviews. We first shared it on [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/pastenlighten/).

## The story of Badshahi Mosque

The name means the Emperor's Mosque, and its history follows the history of Lahore itself, from Mughal glory to neglect and back again.

- **1671 to 1673: built in two years.** The Mughal emperor Aurangzeb ordered the mosque, and his foster brother Fidai Khan Koka, the governor of Lahore, oversaw the work. It was built directly opposite Lahore Fort and its Alamgiri Gate, which was built at the same time.
- **1673 to 1986: the largest mosque in the world.** For more than 300 years no mosque anywhere was bigger. The record finally passed to the Faisal Mosque in Islamabad, which you can read about in our [Faisal Mosque guide](blog/islamabad-faisal-mosque-pakistan-monument.html).
- **From 1799: a stable and barracks.** After Ranjit Singh's army took Lahore, the courtyard was used to keep army horses and the cells around it as soldiers' quarters.
- **1846 to 1852: a British garrison.** When the British took Lahore they too used the mosque as a garrison. In 1852 they set up the Badshahi Mosque Authority to begin returning it to worship.
- **1939 to 1960: the great restoration.** Sir Sikandar Hayat Khan raised funds for major repairs from 1939, and the work was completed in 1960. His tomb stands near the entrance, close to the tomb of the poet Allama Iqbal.
- **1993: on UNESCO's tentative list.** Pakistan put the mosque forward for World Heritage status, alongside its neighbour, Lahore Fort, which is already a World Heritage Site.

For a guide to what to look for inside, from the stairway and the domes to the minarets, see our [top 10 things to see at Badshahi Mosque](blog/top-10-things-badshahi-mosque.html).

## What our guests say

Our tours of Lahore have a 5.0 rating on Google from 39 reviews (November 2026). These are a few of the lines in the reel, in our guests' own words:

*“Bilawal made our day!”* — Mantas G., Google review

*“Bilawal was a God-send on my first day in Lahore as a solo female traveller.”* — A V, Google review

*“We were able to discover the atmosphere and soul of Lahore thanks to his insights, knowledge and hidden stories.”* — Camille JG, Google review

*“He gave us a perspective we would have otherwise missed: a deeper understanding of the fort, the mosque, and the broader history of Pakistan.”* — Rustam A., Google review

You can read every review, in full, on our [reviews page](reviews.html).

## Tips for visiting Badshahi Mosque

- Dress modestly, with shoulders and knees covered. Women should bring a scarf for their hair
- Shoes come off before you enter the courtyard; there is a shoe counter by the steps, and a pair that slips off easily helps
- Visit outside prayer times, and avoid Friday midday, when the mosque fills for Friday prayers
- The red sandstone glows in the late afternoon. Come in the hour before sunset for the best light and photos
- In summer the courtyard stones get very hot, so go early or late in the day
- Ask before photographing people, especially anyone praying
- Lahore Fort is directly opposite, with Hazuri Bagh between them; see our [Lahore Fort guide](blog/top-10-things-lahore-fort.html) and [what to wear in Lahore](blog/what-to-wear-in-lahore.html)

## Frequently asked questions

### When was Badshahi Mosque built?

Badshahi Mosque was built between 1671 and 1673 on the orders of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. The work was overseen by his foster brother Fidai Khan Koka, then governor of Lahore, and the mosque opened in 1673 after only two years of construction.

### Was Badshahi Mosque the largest mosque in the world?

Yes. From its completion in 1673 until 1986, when the Faisal Mosque in Islamabad was finished, it was the largest mosque in the world. It is still the largest mosque built in the Mughal era.

### Can non-Muslims visit Badshahi Mosque?

Yes. Visitors of all faiths are welcome outside prayer times. Dress modestly, take off your shoes at the entrance, and be quiet and respectful near people who are praying. Friday midday prayers are the busiest time, so plan around them.

### What should I wear to Badshahi Mosque?

Cover your shoulders and knees; long trousers or a long skirt and a top with sleeves are ideal. Women should bring a scarf to cover their hair. Shoes come off before the courtyard, so wear a pair that is easy to slip off.

### How long do you need at Badshahi Mosque?

Allow about an hour for the mosque itself. Because Lahore Fort, Hazuri Bagh and the tomb of Allama Iqbal are right next to it, most visitors combine them into a half day.
